description: Eye contact, body language, personal space, Darwin's NVC theory, and Yuki's emoticon study.
content_html:
What Is Non-Verbal Communication?

Non-verbal communication (NVC) refers to all the ways we send and receive messages without using spoken or written words. It includes facial expressions, gestures, posture, touch, eye contact and the use of personal space. Researchers estimate that a large proportion of the meaning in face-to-face interaction comes from non-verbal signals rather than the words used.

Verbal communication uses words — spoken or written — to convey meaning. While verbal communication is precise and can express complex ideas, non-verbal communication operates simultaneously alongside it, often conveying emotion, attitude and relationship information that words alone cannot carry.

Functions of Eye Contact

Eye contact is one of the most studied forms of NVC. It serves three main functions.

First, eye contact helps to regulate the flow of conversation. We use gaze to signal when we are ready to speak, when we want the other person to continue, and when we are handing over our turn. Without these gaze signals, conversations become disorganised and awkward.

Second, eye contact signals attraction. Sustained mutual gaze between two people can indicate romantic interest. Dilated pupils (which happen automatically) and prolonged eye contact are read as signs of interest and liking.

Third, eye contact is a powerful way of expressing emotion. Wide eyes signal surprise or fear; narrowed eyes suggest suspicion or concentration. The eyes are often described as the most expressive part of the face because they are difficult to consciously control.

Body Language

Body language encompasses posture, gesture and touch. Two key posture concepts are open posture and closed posture. Open posture (uncrossed limbs, facing towards the other person) signals openness and positive engagement. Closed posture (crossed arms, turning away) signals defensiveness or discomfort.

Postural echo occurs when a person unconsciously mirrors the body posture of the person they are talking to. This mirroring signals empathy, rapport and liking. We tend to like people who mirror our posture and to mirror the posture of people we feel warmly towards — the process is largely automatic and outside conscious awareness.

Touch is also a component of body language. Touch can convey warmth, reassurance and social bonding, but is highly context-dependent and varies greatly across cultures and relationships.

Key Fact

Eye contact has three main functions: regulating conversation flow, signalling attraction, and expressing emotion. Postural echo (mirroring another’s posture) signals rapport and liking.

Personal space is the zone of distance around a person that they regard as their own. Comfortable distances differ between relationships and contexts. Personal space is not fixed — it varies with culture, gender and social status.

Cultural differences are well-documented: people from some cultures (such as some Mediterranean and Latin American countries) are comfortable with closer personal distance, while people from other cultures (such as northern European or East Asian) typically prefer more distance in interaction. Gender differences also exist: research suggests same-sex pairs of women tend to interact at closer distances than same-sex pairs of men. Higher-status individuals may claim more personal space and feel more comfortable entering others’ zones.

Darwin’s Evolutionary Theory of Non-Verbal Communication

Charles Darwin proposed that many non-verbal behaviours are evolved and adaptive. In his 1872 work on the expression of emotions in humans and animals, Darwin argued that facial expressions and basic emotional displays are innate — they evolved because they enhanced communication and survival, and are therefore universal across human cultures and shared with other species.

Evidence that NVC is innate includes research with neonates (newborn babies). Neonates show basic facial expressions such as disgust and distress from birth, before they have had any opportunity to learn these through observation. The early appearance of these expressions suggests they are biologically programmed rather than culturally learned.

Research on individuals who are sensory deprived — those who are both blind and deaf from birth — provides further evidence. These individuals display many of the same basic emotional expressions as sighted people, even though they cannot have learned them through visual imitation. This strongly suggests an innate biological basis for at least some NVC.

Not all NVC is innate — there is evidence that some aspects are culturally learned. Yuki conducted a study using emoticons (digital faces) to investigate cross-cultural differences in how emotions are read from faces. Yuki showed Japanese and American participants emoticons and asked them to rate the emotional expression. Yuki found that Japanese participants focused more on the eyes when judging emotion, while American participants focused more on the mouth. This led to differences in which emoticons each group rated as expressing happiness or sadness — Japanese emoticons tend to use eye shape to signal emotion (e.g. happy eyes, sad eyes), while American emoticons typically use mouth shape (a smile or frown).

Yuki concluded that the way people read facial expressions is at least partly culturally learned, not purely innate. If NVC were entirely innate, people from different cultures would read the same features in the same way. The fact that Japanese and American participants read faces differently suggests cultural learning shapes how we interpret non-verbal signals.

Key Fact

Yuki found that Japanese participants focused on the eyes and American participants on the mouth when reading emotional emoticons. This cross-cultural difference in reading faces suggests that some NVC is learned rather than purely innate, supporting the nurture side of the debate.

The Nature–Nurture Debate in NVC

The evidence on NVC points to a combination of nature and nurture. Basic emotional expressions appear to be innate (supported by neonate research and sensory-deprived individuals). However, the way people interpret and display NVC is shaped by cultural learning and social norms (supported by Yuki). Most psychologists today accept that NVC involves both biological foundations and cultural variation.
exam_tip_html: For 9-mark questions on NVC, do not confuse ‘evidence it is innate’ with ‘evidence it is learned’ — you need to cover both for a top-band answer. Remember: innate evidence = neonates and sensory-deprived individuals; learned evidence = Yuki’s emoticon study. For ‘describe a study’ questions on Yuki, state the cross-cultural difference clearly: Japanese = eyes; American = mouth.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Non-verbal communication includes eye contact (regulating conversation, signalling attraction, expressing emotion), body language (open/closed posture, postural echo, touch) and personal space (varying by culture, gender and status).
  • Darwin argued NVC is evolved and adaptive; evidence from neonates and sensory-deprived individuals supports an innate biological basis for basic emotional expressions.
  • Yuki’s emoticon study found Japanese participants focused on eyes and American participants on mouth, suggesting cultural learning shapes how we read NVC — supporting the nurture side of the innate-versus-learned debate.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes postural echo?
A) Using eye contact to signal the end of your speaking turn
B) Keeping a comfortable distance from another person
C) Unconsciously mirroring another person's body posture
D) Crossing your arms to signal disagreement
practice_questions.marks: C) Unconsciously mirroring another person's body posture [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define 'personal space' in the context of non-verbal communication.
practice_questions.marks: Personal space is the invisible zone or boundary around a person [1 mark] that they consider their own, and within which they feel comfortable or uncomfortable depending on who enters it [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe one piece of evidence that suggests non-verbal communication is innate.
practice_questions.marks: Research with neonates (newborn babies) provides evidence that NVC is innate [1 mark]. Neonates display basic facial expressions such as disgust and distress from birth, before they have had any opportunity to learn these through observation or imitation [1 mark]. The early appearance of these expressions suggests they are biologically programmed rather than culturally acquired [1 mark]. [OR: sensory-deprived individuals show the same emotional expressions as sighted people, supporting an innate basis — accept either example fully developed.]

practice_questions.text: A person at a party stands with arms crossed, avoiding eye contact, and stays as far from others as possible. Using your knowledge of non-verbal communication, explain what their behaviour might be communicating.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two NVC concepts precisely identified and linked to the scenario (e.g. closed posture — crossed arms signal defensiveness or discomfort, indicating unwillingness to engage; avoidance of eye contact signals lack of interest or discomfort in social interaction; maximising personal space suggests a desire to limit close social contact).
Secure: One NVC concept clearly explained and linked to the behaviour described.
Developing: Names a relevant NVC concept but does not explain how it applies to the specific behaviour in the scenario.
Emerging: Vague statements about body language or shyness without psychological framing.

practice_questions.text: Describe Yuki's study of emoticons as evidence about non-verbal communication.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate aim (to investigate cross-cultural differences in reading emotional expressions from faces), method (Japanese and American participants rated emoticons for emotional expression), results (Japanese focused on eyes; Americans focused on mouth; different emoticon conventions in each culture), and conclusion (reading NVC is at least partly culturally learned, not purely innate) — all four elements.
Secure: Three elements described accurately.
Developing: Two elements or one in good detail; some inaccuracy.
Emerging: Vague account with limited specific detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the debate over whether non-verbal communication is innate or learned.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of Darwin's evolutionary theory (evolved and adaptive); innate evidence (neonates, sensory-deprived); learned evidence (Yuki — cross-cultural differences in reading faces); evaluation includes at least two developed points (e.g. neonate research controlled for learning, supporting innate basis; Yuki shows cultural variation, supporting nurture; modern consensus is interaction of both; limitation of Yuki — emoticons are artificial stimuli).
Secure: Both sides of the debate described; evaluation covers two points with some development.
Developing: One side of the debate described; evaluation underdeveloped.
Emerging: Brief description of one position; minimal evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: In Yuki's emoticon study, which facial feature did Japanese participants focus on when reading emotional expressions?
Which of the following provides evidence that non-verbal communication has an innate basis?
options: Yuki's emoticon study showing cultural variation
Neonates displaying basic facial expressions from birth
Adults learning to interpret new NVC signals

knowledge_checks.q: Open posture involves relaxed, uncrossed limbs and signals _____ and willingness to engage.
_____ echo is the unconscious mirroring of another person's posture, which signals rapport and liking.
Match each NVC concept to its description:
right: Relaxed, uncrossed limbs signalling approachability and engagement
Crossed limbs or turning away, signalling defensiveness
Unconsciously mirroring another's posture, signalling rapport

flashcard_questions.a: Communication that does not use words — includes facial expressions, gestures, eye contact, posture and personal space.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the three functions of eye contact.
flashcard_questions.a: Regulating conversation flow, signalling attraction, and expressing emotion.

flashcard_questions.q: What does an open posture — relaxed, uncrossed limbs facing towards the other person — signal in non-verbal communication?
flashcard_questions.a: It signals that the person is approachable and willing to engage, conveying a positive, non-threatening attitude.
Defensiveness, discomfort or unwillingness to engage.
Unconsciously mirroring another person's posture, signalling rapport and liking.
The invisible boundary around a person that they consider their own.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Darwin argue about non-verbal communication?
flashcard_questions.a: NVC is evolved and adaptive — it evolved through natural selection to enhance communication and survival.

flashcard_questions.q: What evidence from neonates supports an innate basis for NVC?
flashcard_questions.a: Newborns display basic facial expressions like disgust and distress before any opportunity to learn them.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Yuki find in his emoticon study?
flashcard_questions.a: Japanese participants focused on eyes; American participants focused on mouths when reading emotion.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Yuki conclude about NVC?
flashcard_questions.a: Reading facial expressions is at least partly culturally learned, not purely innate.

flashcard_questions.q: How do sensory-deprived individuals support an innate basis for NVC?
flashcard_questions.a: People blind and deaf from birth display the same basic emotional expressions as sighted people.

glossary_terms.definition: Communication that does not use words, including facial expressions, gestures, eye contact, posture, touch and personal space.
Communication that uses words, either spoken or written, to convey meaning.
A body posture in which the limbs are relaxed and uncrossed, indicating openness, approachability and willingness to engage.
A body posture in which the limbs are crossed or turned away, indicating defensiveness, discomfort or unwillingness to engage.
The unconscious mirroring of another person's body posture, which signals rapport and liking.
The invisible boundary around a person that they consider their own, and within which they feel comfortable or uncomfortable depending on who enters it.
Having evolved through natural selection because they enhanced survival and reproductive success in ancestral environments.
